disease.name: Food Poisoning
disease.scientific_name: Foodborne Illness / Foodborne Disease / Foodborne Intoxication
disease.icd_10_code: A00-A09 (Intestinal Infectious Diseases); A02 (Salmonella); A04 (Other bacterial intestinal infections); A05 (Other bacterial foodborne intoxications); T61-T65 (Toxic effects of substances — chemical/toxin food poisoning); K52.9 (Non-infective gastroenteritis)
disease.category: Infectious Disease / Gastrointestinal Disease / Public Health Emergency

overview.description: Food poisoning (foodborne illness) is a broad term encompassing illness caused by consuming food or beverages contaminated with pathogenic bacteria, viruses, parasites, or their toxins, as well as chemical contaminants or natural toxins. It is one of the most common and preventable public health problems globally, manifesting predominantly as gastrointestinal illness — nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps — but potentially progressing to life-threatening complications including severe dehydration, septicaemia, haemolytic uraemic syndrome, neurological damage, and multi-organ failure. Symptoms typically begin within hours to days of consuming contaminated food and range from mild, self-limiting gastroenteritis to medical emergencies requiring intensive care.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the gastrointestinal tract (stomach, small intestine, large intestine); systemically in severe cases: kidneys, liver, brain, blood, and nervous system
overview.prevalence: WHO estimates 600 million illnesses and 420,000 deaths globally per year; 1 in 10 people worldwide are affected annually; 125,000 deaths annually in children under 5 years.
overview.age_group: All ages; children under 5, elderly over 65, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals at highest risk for severe disease.
overview.is_contagious_note: Many foodborne illnesses are person-to-person transmissible (norovirus, hepatitis A, typhoid) in addition to food-borne transmission
overview.key_fact: Approximately 90% of foodborne illnesses could be prevented with proper food safety practices

types.name: Bacterial Food Poisoning
types.description: The most common cause of foodborne illness — accounting for the majority of food poisoning outbreaks worldwide. Bacteria contaminate food either before consumption (and multiply if food is improperly stored) or produce heat-stable toxins in food before it is eaten. Divided into: infective (bacteria invade intestinal mucosa — e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter) and toxin-mediated (pre-formed toxin in food — e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus).

major_organisms.symptoms: Diarrhoea (watery to mucoid), fever, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting
major_organisms.severity: Mild to moderate; can be severe/fatal in infants, elderly, immunocompromised
major_organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration; antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, azithromycin) only for severe/systemic disease
major_organisms.complications: Bacteraemia, reactive arthritis, typhoid fever (Salmonella Typhi)

major_organisms.symptoms: Profuse watery or bloody diarrhoea, severe abdominal cramps, fever, nausea, vomiting
major_organisms.severity: Usually self-limiting; severe in elderly and immunocompromised
major_organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration; azithromycin or ciprofloxacin for severe cases
major_organisms.complications: MOST COMMON trigger of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS); reactive arthritis; post-infectious IBS
major_organisms.note: Most common bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in high-income countries

major_organisms.organism: Escherichia coli (E. coli) — particularly STEC O157:H7
major_organisms.symptoms: Severe bloody diarrhoea, severe abdominal cramps, low-grade fever or no fever
major_organisms.severity: Can be life-threatening — Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (HUS) develops in 5-10% of children
major_organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration; antibiotics CONTRAINDICATED in STEC O157:H7 (increases HUS risk)
major_organisms.complications: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (HUS) — life-threatening triad of haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney failure; especially in children
major_organisms.warning: Do NOT give antibiotics or antidiarrheals (loperamide) for E. coli O157:H7

foods: Deli meats — food left at room temperature
major_organisms.incubation: 1-6 hours (very short — toxin pre-formed in food)
major_organisms.symptoms: Explosive vomiting (dominant), nausea, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea; RARELY fever
major_organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration; antiemetics; antibiotics NOT required (toxin-mediated)
major_organisms.note: Toxin is heat-stable — cooking food after contamination does not destroy the toxin

major_organisms.foods_emetic: Reheated fried rice, pasta, cooked cereals left at room temperature (Emetic syndrome — rice dish left out after cooking)
major_organisms.foods_diarrhoeal: Meat products, vegetable dishes, sauces (Diarrhoeal syndrome)
major_organisms.symptoms_diarrhoeal: Watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramps — mild or no vomiting
major_organisms.treatment: Supportive care only; oral rehydration
major_organisms.note: Classic cause of 'Chinese takeaway food poisoning' — reheated rice syndrome; emetic toxin cereulide is heat-stable

foods: Cooked meat dishes (especially beef, poultry, gravy)
Stews — prepared in bulk and cooled slowly
major_organisms.symptoms: Sudden watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramping; vomiting uncommon; no fever
major_organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration
major_organisms.note: Spores survive cooking and germinate as food cools slowly — kept warm between 20-50°C

major_organisms.symptoms: Descending FLACCID paralysis — ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, respiratory failure; NO diarrhoea typically; minimal fever; toxin already in food
major_organisms.duration: Weeks to months (requires ventilatory support in severe cases)
major_organisms.severity: POTENTIALLY FATAL — respiratory paralysis; 5-10% case fatality rate
major_organisms.treatment: IV/IM heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (HBAT); ICU respiratory support; mechanical ventilation if needed
major_organisms.note: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — descending paralysis is characteristic; do NOT give antidiarrheals; report immediately to public health

major_organisms.incubation: 3-70 days (median ~21 days — very long; called 'the great mimic')
major_organisms.symptoms: Mild: flu-like illness; fever, muscle aches. Severe (invasive): meningitis, septicaemia, encephalitis; in pregnancy: foetal loss, premature birth, neonatal meningitis
major_organisms.severity: High mortality (20-30%) in at-risk groups; ESPECIALLY DANGEROUS in pregnancy, elderly, immunocompromised
major_organisms.treatment: IV ampicillin + gentamicin (combination therapy for severe/invasive listeriosis)
major_organisms.note: Grows at refrigerator temperatures (4°C) — unlike most bacteria; this makes it particularly dangerous in chilled foods

foods: Raw or undercooked seafood — oysters, clams, shrimp, crabs
major_organisms.symptoms: Vibrio para: watery/bloody diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, fever, nausea, vomiting. Cholera: profuse watery diarrhoea ('rice water stools'), vomiting, rapid dehydration — NO fever
major_organisms.severity: Cholera: life-threatening dehydration (can lose 10-20L fluid/day); case fatality >50% without treatment; <1% with early ORT
major_organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration (IV for severe cholera); tetracycline, azithromycin, or ciprofloxacin for cholera

major_organisms.symptoms: Watery diarrhoea → bloody mucoid diarrhoea (dysentery), tenesmus, fever, abdominal cramping
major_organisms.treatment: Ciprofloxacin or azithromycin; ORS
major_organisms.complications: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (rare — Shigella dysenteriae type 1); toxic megacolon; reactive arthritis

foods: Raw vegetables washed in contaminated water
major_organisms.symptoms: Stepwise rising fever, relative bradycardia, headache, malaise, abdominal pain, rose spots (skin rash), hepatosplenomegaly, constipation or diarrhoea
major_organisms.severity: Can be fatal without treatment; 1-4% case fatality rate untreated
major_organisms.treatment: Azithromycin, ceftriaxone, or ciprofloxacin (check local resistance patterns)

types.name: Viral Food Poisoning
types.description: Viruses are responsible for a majority of all foodborne illnesses in high-income countries. Person-to-person transmission is also common (faecal-oral route). Viral food poisoning typically causes shorter illness duration than bacterial but can be very disabling.

foods: Ready-to-eat foods handled by infected food workers
major_organisms.symptoms: Explosive vomiting (projectile), watery diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal cramps, low-grade fever, headache, myalgia
major_organisms.severity: Usually self-limiting; can be severe in elderly and immunocompromised; dehydration risk especially in very young children
major_organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration only; no antiviral treatment; antibiotics NOT useful
major_organisms.note: MOST COMMON cause of acute viral gastroenteritis worldwide — responsible for 50% of all food-borne outbreaks globally; very contagious (18 viral particles sufficient for infection); survives up to 2 weeks on surfaces; chlorine-resistant; highly transmissible person-to-person

major_organisms.symptoms: Profuse watery diarrhoea (yellow-green colour), vomiting, fever, dehydration
major_organisms.severity: Most severe in children under 5 — leading viral cause of severe childhood diarrhoea and dehydration globally before widespread vaccination
major_organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration; hospitalisation if severe dehydration
major_organisms.prevention: Rotavirus vaccine highly effective (Rotarix, RotaTeq) — dramatically reduced rotavirus hospitalisation in vaccinated countries

foods: Food handled by infected food workers
major_organisms.symptoms: Prodrome: fever, nausea, anorexia, malaise. Then: jaundice (yellowing), dark urine, pale stools, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly
major_organisms.severity: Usually self-limiting; case fatality rate <0.1% in young adults; 1.8% over age 50; fulminant hepatic failure rare
major_organisms.treatment: Supportive care; no antiviral treatment; rest, hydration, avoid alcohol
major_organisms.prevention: Hepatitis A vaccine (2 doses); highly effective

foods: Undercooked pork, wild boar meat (zoonotic HEV genotype 3)
major_organisms.symptoms: Fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice
major_organisms.severity: ESPECIALLY DANGEROUS in pregnancy — case fatality rate 20-25% in pregnant women (3rd trimester); can cause fulminant hepatic failure and foetal loss
major_organisms.treatment: Supportive care; ribavirin for severe/chronic cases in immunocompromised
major_organisms.note: Leading cause of acute hepatitis in developing countries including India; waterborne outbreaks common

types.name: Parasitic Food and Waterborne Illness
types.description: Parasites causing food and waterborne illness range from single-celled protozoa to multi-cellular helminths (worms). Parasitic infections are particularly common in areas with poor sanitation and contaminated water supplies. Onset is typically delayed compared to bacterial and viral food poisoning.

major_organisms.symptoms: Bloody mucoid diarrhoea (dysentery), tenesmus, abdominal cramps; invasive: amoebic liver abscess (right upper quadrant pain, fever, tender hepatomegaly)
major_organisms.treatment: Metronidazole 500-750mg three times daily for 5-10 days; followed by luminal agent (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin)
major_organisms.complications: Amoebic liver abscess — most common extraintestinal complication; amoebic colitis; perforation; toxic megacolon

major_organisms.route: Contaminated water (most common — cysts highly chlorine-resistant); food; person-to-person
major_organisms.symptoms: Chronic watery or greasy diarrhoea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramps, sulphur burps, weight loss; NO blood in stool
major_organisms.treatment: Metronidazole 400mg three times daily for 5-7 days; tinidazole 2g single dose; nitazoxanide
major_organisms.note: Most common intestinal protozoal infection globally; traveller's diarrhoea cause

major_organisms.route: Contaminated water (chlorine-resistant oocysts); person-to-person; contact with animals
major_organisms.symptoms: Watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever; immunocompromised: severe chronic diarrhoea
major_organisms.treatment: Nitazoxanide (immunocompetent); no reliable treatment in severe immunosuppression; ORS
major_organisms.note: Chlorine-resistant in swimming pools and water supplies; major cause of waterborne outbreaks

major_organisms.route: Undercooked pork, wild boar, bear meat
major_organisms.incubation: 1-2 days GI phase; 2-8 weeks systemic phase
major_organisms.symptoms: GI phase: diarrhoea, vomiting. Systemic phase: periorbital oedema, myalgia, fever, headache, splinter haemorrhages
major_organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole; corticosteroids for severe myositis

major_organisms.route: T. solium from undercooked pork; T. saginata from undercooked beef
major_organisms.symptoms: Usually asymptomatic; abdominal discomfort, weight loss, proglottids in stool; neurocysticercosis (T. solium larvae in brain — seizures, headache)
major_organisms.treatment: Praziquantel; niclosamide

types.name: Toxin-Mediated Food Poisoning (Preformed Toxins)
types.description: Caused by consuming food already containing preformed toxins produced by bacteria, fungi, algae, or fish. Toxins are often heat-stable and are NOT destroyed by cooking food after contamination. Characteristically has very short incubation period (minutes to hours). No viable bacteria need to be present — the toxin alone causes illness.

major_toxins.source: Staphylococcus aureus pre-formed in warm food
major_toxins.features: Explosive vomiting, nausea; toxin heat-stable at 100°C for 30 min — cooking AFTER contamination does NOT help

major_toxins.toxin: Botulinum Toxin (Types A, B, E, F)
major_toxins.source: Clostridium botulinum in anaerobic conditions (canned/preserved foods)
major_toxins.features: Descending flaccid paralysis; ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, respiratory failure; MEDICAL EMERGENCY

major_toxins.source: Large reef fish (barracuda, grouper, snapper, tuna) from tropical/subtropical waters
major_toxins.features: GI symptoms PLUS neurological: peripheral paresthesias (burning/numbness), TEMPERATURE REVERSAL (cold feels hot — pathognomonic), reversal of sensory perceptions, bradycardia, hypotension; toxin heat-stable — not destroyed by cooking
major_toxins.treatment: Supportive; IV mannitol may help neurological symptoms; avoid alcohol and nut consumption (worsens symptoms for months)

major_toxins.source: Improperly refrigerated scombroid fish (tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi, swordfish) — bacteria convert histidine to histamine
major_toxins.features: Flushing, urticaria (hives), burning/metallic taste in mouth, GI symptoms, headache, palpitations — MIMICS ALLERGIC REACTION; fever may be present; normal IgE (not true allergy)
major_toxins.treatment: Antihistamines (diphenhydramine, cetirizine); epinephrine if severe; resolves in 24 hours

major_toxins.source: Shellfish (mussels, clams, oysters, scallops) from harmful algal bloom areas
major_toxins.features: Oral and perioral paresthesias (tingling), numbness, ataxia, muscle weakness, respiratory paralysis
major_toxins.treatment: Supportive; ICU respiratory support; no specific antidote

major_toxins.source: Mouldy maize, groundnuts (peanuts), tree nuts, dried spices
major_toxins.features: Acute: hepatotoxicity, jaundice; Chronic: most potent natural carcinogen — hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer)

types.name: Chemical Food Poisoning
types.description: Caused by chemical contaminants in food — including pesticide residues, heavy metals, industrial chemicals, and food additive reactions. Often presents with rapid onset and may involve neurological or systemic symptoms beyond the GI tract.

examples.source: Pesticide residues on unwashed fruits and vegetables
examples.symptoms: DUMBELS: Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis (small pupils), Bradycardia/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation; muscle fasciculations, seizures
examples.treatment: Atropine (antidote for muscarinic effects); pralidoxime (2-PAM) for organophosphates; decontamination

examples.chemical: Heavy Metal Poisoning (Lead, Mercury, Cadmium, Arsenic)
examples.source: Contaminated water, acidic foods in old tin cans, fish (mercury), contaminated soil
examples.symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, metallic taste; chronic: neurological damage, kidney disease
examples.treatment: Chelation therapy (DMSA, BAL, EDTA) for acute poisoning

examples.source: Excessive nitrite-cured meats; contaminated well water
examples.symptoms: Cyanosis (blue skin), headache, dizziness, dyspnoea; blood becomes chocolate brown

types.name: Mushroom Poisoning (Mycetism)
types.description: Caused by ingestion of toxic mushrooms. Ranges from mild GI symptoms to life-threatening liver failure. The most dangerous mushroom toxin globally is Amatoxin (from Amanita phalloides — Death Cap mushroom).

types.toxin: Amatoxins (Amanita phalloides — Death Cap, Amanita ocreata, Galerina marginata)
types.incubation: 6-24 hours GI phase; liver failure 3-5 days
types.features: Phase 1 (6-24h): Choleriform — profuse vomiting, watery diarrhoea, severe abdominal cramps; Phase 2 (24-72h): Apparent recovery (false improvement); Phase 3 (3-7 days): Fulminant hepatic and renal failure; HIGHLY FATAL
types.treatment: Activated charcoal early; IV silibinin (milk thistle extract); N-acetylcysteine; liver transplant in severe cases

types.features: DUMBELS syndrome: salivation, lacrimation, sweating, miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm

types.toxin: Ibotenic acid / Muscimol (Amanita muscaria — Fly Agaric)

severity_levels.name: Mild Food Poisoning
severity_levels.description: Self-limiting illness with minimal dehydration and no systemic involvement
severity_levels.symptoms: Nausea, mild vomiting (1-3 episodes), mild watery diarrhoea (3-5 loose stools/day), mild abdominal cramps; no blood in stool; no fever or low-grade fever (<38°C)
severity_levels.dehydration: None or minimal — urine still normal colour and frequency
severity_levels.functional_impact: Some discomfort; most daily activities still possible
severity_levels.management: Home management with oral rehydration; BRAT diet; rest; no antibiotics needed; resolves within 24-48 hours
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: If symptoms persist beyond 48-72 hours, fever rises, blood appears in stool, or dehydration develops

severity_levels.name: Moderate Food Poisoning
severity_levels.description: Significant GI illness with moderate dehydration requiring medical evaluation
severity_levels.symptoms: Persistent vomiting (>3-5 episodes) preventing adequate fluid intake; diarrhoea >5-10 loose stools/day; abdominal cramps; fever 38-39°C; possible mucus in stool
severity_levels.dehydration: Moderate — decreased urine output, dry mouth, moderate thirst, mild dizziness on standing
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to work or carry out normal activities; bed rest required
severity_levels.management: GP or urgent care review; oral rehydration with ORS; possible antiemetics; blood tests if indicated; consider antibiotic if specific bacteria suspected; monitor for worsening
severity_levels.who_needs_medical_attention: High-risk groups: children <2 years, elderly >65, pregnant women, immunocompromised, chronic illness

severity_levels.name: Severe Food Poisoning
severity_levels.description: Severe GI illness with significant dehydration, systemic illness, or bloody diarrhoea requiring hospitalisation
severity_levels.symptoms: Persistent bloody or mucoid diarrhoea; high fever >39°C; severe vomiting; signs of dehydration; inability to tolerate any fluids; confusion or altered consciousness
severity_levels.dehydration: Severe — significantly reduced urine output (<0.5 mL/kg/hour), sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, hypotension, skin tenting
severity_levels.management: Emergency department attendance; IV fluid resuscitation; blood cultures; stool cultures; IV antibiotics as guided by microbiology; monitoring for complications (HUS, bacteraemia, organ failure)
severity_levels.emergency_criteria: Signs of sepsis, signs of peritonitis, neurological symptoms (botulism), pregnancy complications, age extremes

severity_levels.name: Critical / Life-Threatening Food Poisoning
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening complications including septicaemia, multi-organ failure, neurological involvement (botulism), HUS, or toxic megacolon
severity_levels.examples: Botulism with respiratory paralysis; STEC O157:H7 with HUS; Listeria meningitis; Amanita mushroom poisoning with liver failure; Cholera with extreme dehydration; Typhoid perforation
severity_levels.management: ICU admission; intensive monitoring; organ-specific treatment; specialist input (nephrology, hepatology, neurology as needed); antitoxin for botulism; liver transplant for fulminant hepatic failure
severity_levels.mortality: Varies by pathogen — Botulism: 5-10%; Listeria: 20-30%; Amanita poisoning: up to 30% without liver transplant

causative_agents_overview.bacteria: 50-70% of identifiable foodborne illness in high-income countries; Campylobacter, Salmonella, Staphylococcus aureus, E. coli, Listeria, Clostridium most important
causative_agents_overview.viruses: Responsible for majority of food poisoning outbreaks by number; Norovirus most common cause globally
causative_agents_overview.parasites: Major cause in low-to-middle income countries; Entamoeba, Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Taenia
causative_agents_overview.toxins: Pre-formed toxins in food (Staph, B. cereus, Botulinum, fish toxins)

routes_of_contamination.description: The MOST COMMON cause of food poisoning. Bacterial multiplication occurs most rapidly between 5°C and 63°C (the 'Danger Zone'). Food left in this temperature range for more than 2 hours allows dangerous levels of bacterial growth.
examples: Cooked food left at room temperature >2 hours before serving
Slow cooling of large batches of food
Hot food not maintained above 63°C during service

routes_of_contamination.description: Transfer of pathogens from one food (usually raw) to another (usually cooked/ready-to-eat) through direct contact, contaminated equipment, or food handlers' hands.
examples: Raw meat juices contaminating ready-to-eat foods
Using same chopping board for raw chicken and salad vegetables
Hands contaminated with raw meat touching cooked food
Raw and cooked foods stored together in refrigerator

routes_of_contamination.description: Insufficient cooking temperatures fail to kill pathogens in food. Different foods require specific internal temperature targets.

safe_internal_temperatures.eggs_dishes: Yolk and white firm; ≥71°C egg dishes

routes_of_contamination.description: Untreated or contaminated water used for drinking, cooking, or irrigation of crops. Major cause in developing countries. Cryptosporidium and Giardia resistant to standard chlorination.
examples: Drinking untreated well, river, or stream water
Raw vegetables irrigated with contaminated water or sewage effluent

routes_of_contamination.description: Infected food handlers are a major source of foodborne outbreaks — particularly for norovirus, hepatitis A, typhoid, and Shigella. Inadequate handwashing is the primary pathway.
examples: Not washing hands after using toilet
Handling food while ill with gastroenteritis
Not washing hands after handling raw meat before touching other foods
Working while symptomatic with norovirus or diarrhoea

routes_of_contamination.description: Improper storage conditions promote bacterial growth and toxin formation.
examples: Leaving cooked food uncovered at room temperature
Storing raw meat above cooked food in refrigerator
Thawing frozen food at room temperature
Storing dry goods in damp conditions (aflatoxin production in mould)

routes_of_contamination.description: Pathogens present in animals before slaughter (Salmonella, Campylobacter in poultry), in farm environment, or in water used for irrigation.
examples: Salmonella/Campylobacter naturally present in chicken gut
E. coli O157:H7 in cattle gut
Norovirus in shellfish filtering contaminated sewage
HAV in shellfish from polluted waters

risk_factors: Consuming raw or undercooked meat, poultry, seafood, or eggs
Eating at street food stalls or establishments with poor hygiene practices
Consuming raw shellfish (oysters, clams, mussels — concentrate viral and bacterial pathogens from water)
Drinking untreated or unboiled water in areas with poor sanitation
International travel to areas with different food safety standards (traveller's diarrhoea)
Eating food prepared in bulk (institutional catering, weddings, parties) with slow cooling
Consuming unpasteurised dairy products (raw milk, soft fresh cheese)
Age <5 years or >65 years — higher susceptibility and risk of severe disease
Pregnancy — altered immunity, Listeria risk specifically
Immunosuppression — HIV, chemotherapy, organ transplants, high-dose corticosteroids
Chronic conditions — liver disease, diabetes, gastrointestinal disease
Eating during the summer (warmer temperatures accelerate bacterial growth — food poisoning peaks June-September in northern hemisphere)
Not washing hands before eating or after using the bathroom
Home food preservation (canning, fermenting) without proper technique (Botulism risk)

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea
primary_symptoms.description: Sensation of stomach upset and urge to vomit — typically one of the earliest symptoms of food poisoning. Onset time after eating contaminated food is an important diagnostic clue: nausea within 1-6 hours suggests Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus (toxin pre-formed in food); nausea after 6-24 hours suggests bacterial infection; nausea after 1-5 days suggests viral illness or bacterial invasion.
primary_symptoms.onset: Minutes to hours to days after consuming contaminated food depending on causative agent

primary_symptoms.name: Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Forceful expulsion of stomach contents — a protective mechanism to eliminate toxins. Can be explosive and projectile (characteristic of norovirus and Staphylococcus toxin). Repeated vomiting leads to dehydration, electrolyte loss, and inability to retain oral fluids or medications.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Profuse vomiting is the hallmark of norovirus and staph food poisoning; repeated vomiting requiring IV fluids is an emergency sign in at-risk populations

primary_symptoms.name: Diarrhoea
primary_symptoms.description: Loose or liquid stools, often frequent (>3 times in 24 hours meeting definition). Character varies by pathogen: Watery diarrhoea = non-invasive bacteria (toxin-mediated: Staph, B. cereus, Vibrio cholerae), viruses. Bloody diarrhoea (dysentery) = invasive bacteria: Shigella, Campylobacter, STEC E. coli, Entamoeba. Rice water stools = Vibrio cholerae. Greasy floating stools = Giardia.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Severe — major cause of dangerous fluid/electrolyte loss
primary_symptoms.note: Presence of blood in diarrhoea is an important warning sign — requires prompt medical evaluation; loperamide CONTRAINDICATED with bloody diarrhoea

primary_symptoms.name: Abdominal Cramps and Pain
primary_symptoms.description: Crampy, colicky abdominal pain — typically periumbilical or diffuse. Caused by intestinal hyperperistalsis as the gut attempts to expel contaminated contents. Severe constant abdominal pain (not colicky) with guarding or rigidity suggests complications (peritonitis, ileus, toxic megacolon) — emergency sign.
primary_symptoms.onset: Concurrent with nausea and vomiting or diarrhoea

primary_symptoms.name: Fever
primary_symptoms.description: Elevated body temperature indicates systemic inflammatory response to infection — distinguishes INFECTIVE food poisoning (bacteria invading intestinal wall, entering bloodstream) from TOXIN-MEDIATED (Staph, B. cereus) where fever is minimal or absent. High fever (>39°C) in food poisoning suggests invasive bacterial disease and possible bacteraemia/septicaemia.
primary_symptoms.severity: Low-grade (<38.5°C) in most to High (>39°C) in invasive bacterial infection
primary_symptoms.note: ABSENCE of fever with vomiting suggests toxin-mediated (Staph, B. cereus); PRESENCE of high fever with bloody diarrhoea suggests Shigella, Campylobacter, or invasive Salmonella

primary_symptoms.name: Dehydration Signs
primary_symptoms.description: Progressive loss of body fluids and electrolytes from vomiting and diarrhoea leads to dehydration — the major cause of food poisoning deaths worldwide (especially in children). Signs of dehydration: mild (increased thirst, darker urine); moderate (dry mouth, sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, decreased urine); severe (very sunken eyes, no urination, cold/clammy extremities, rapid weak pulse, confusion/altered consciousness).
primary_symptoms.onset: Develops over hours with repeated vomiting/diarrhoea
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Dehydration assessment guides management — mild: oral rehydration; severe: IV fluids

secondary_symptoms: Headache — common with systemic illness and dehydration; very prominent in typhoid fever (frontal headache)
Fatigue and malaise — general weakness from infection, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance
Loss of appetite (anorexia) — very common; early symptom in hepatitis A
Bloating and excessive flatulence — particularly in Giardia infection
Foul-smelling, greasy, or floating stools (steatorrhoea) — fat malabsorption in Giardia
Mucus in stool — invasive colitis (Shigella, Campylobacter, Entamoeba)
Jaundice (yellowing of skin/eyes) — hepatitis A or E; Amanita mushroom poisoning
Dark urine (bilirubinuria) — hepatitis; haemolysis in HUS
Pale/clay-coloured stools — biliary obstruction from hepatitis
Skin flushing, urticaria (hives) — scombroid (histamine) poisoning or allergic-type food reactions
Temperature reversal (cold feels hot, hot feels cold) — pathognomonic for ciguatera toxin poisoning
Neurological symptoms (ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, weakness) — BOTULISM WARNING SIGNS
Rose spots (faint salmon-pink flat spots on trunk) — typhoid fever
warning_signs_of_attack: Blood in stool (red or dark tarry) — possible invasive bacterial infection, HUS, or bowel ischaemia; REQUIRES MEDICAL ATTENTION
Signs of severe dehydration: no urination for 8+ hours, confusion, rapid weak pulse, cold extremities — MEDICAL EMERGENCY
Neurological symptoms: double vision (diplopia), ptosis (drooping eyelid), difficulty swallowing, slurred speech, progressive weakness — possible BOTULISM — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES
High fever >39°C with abdominal pain — possible bacteraemia or septicaemia
No improvement after 3-4 days — possible typhoid, parasitic infection, or serious complication
Sudden sharp generalised abdominal pain with guarding or rigidity — possible bowel perforation
Jaundice (yellow skin/eyes) appearing — hepatitis A/E, liver failure (Amanita poisoning)
Decreased or no urine output after 12-24 hours — possible acute kidney injury (HUS, severe dehydration)
symptoms_in_children: Signs of dehydration develop much faster in children than adults — sunken fontanelle (infants), sunken eyes, no tears when crying, very dry mouth, no wet nappies for 6+ hours
Children often cannot describe symptoms specifically — watch for: irritability, listlessness, not passing urine, refusing to drink, pale or mottled skin
Fever tends to be higher in children (can reach 40°C) — febrile seizures are a risk
Diarrhoea frequency normal for infants is up to 8 times daily — compare with child's usual pattern
Projectile vomiting in infants — may indicate pyloric stenosis (not food poisoning) — if no diarrhoea and only vomiting in first 8 weeks of life, see doctor urgently
Weight loss is an important indicator — weigh before and after illness if possible
Return to school: child should remain at home for 48 hours after last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting

incubation_period_guide.description: The time between eating contaminated food and symptom onset is a key diagnostic clue for identifying the likely pathogen.

guide.likely_cause: Chemical poisoning; heavy metals; seafood toxins (scombroid)
Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin; Bacillus cereus emetic toxin; chemical poisoning
Bacillus cereus diarrhoeal toxin; Clostridium perfringens; Vibrio parahaemolyticus
Salmonella; Campylobacter; E. coli; Listeria (early GI phase); Vibrio cholerae; Norovirus
Campylobacter; Salmonella; Shigella; Yersinia; STEC E. coli O157:H7; Giardia (early)
Giardia; Hepatitis A; Listeria invasive; Typhoid fever
Hepatitis A; Hepatitis E; Entamoeba histolytica; Parasitic infections

medical_history: Detailed food history: all foods and drinks consumed in the preceding 24-72 hours (up to 7 days for longer incubation pathogens); list every item including condiments, sauces, and water source
Timing of food consumption and symptom onset — calculate incubation period (key diagnostic clue)
Others affected: family members, friends, or coworkers who ate the same food and are ill (outbreak investigation)
Source of food: restaurant, home-cooked, street food, takeaway, buffet, picnic, institutional food
Recent travel history: abroad or to a different region (traveller's diarrhoea; enteric fever; hepatitis A/E; Giardia; Entamoeba)
Water source: tap (treated), bottled, well, river, swimming pool
Occupational history: healthcare worker, food handler, childcare (Shigella, Cryptosporidium, Norovirus)
Contact with farm animals or pets (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium, Yersinia)
Specific food risk: raw shellfish (norovirus, HAV, Vibrio), raw milk (Listeria, Campylobacter, Salmonella), undercooked poultry (Campylobacter, Salmonella), home-preserved foods (Botulism), mushrooms
Current medications: immunosuppressants, antibiotics (C. difficile risk), proton pump inhibitors (reduce gastric acid barrier — increases infection risk)
Medical history: inflammatory bowel disease, HIV, recent antibiotic course, prior GI surgery, immunosuppression
physical_examination: Vital signs: temperature, heart rate, blood pressure (supine and standing — orthostatic changes indicate dehydration), respiratory rate, oxygen saturation
Hydration assessment: mucous membrane moisture, skin turgor (pinch skin over clavicle or dorsum of hand), sunken eyes, capillary refill time

Abdominal examination: inspection (distension), auscultation (hyperactive vs absent bowel sounds), percussion (tympany), palpation (tenderness location, guarding, rigidity, peritonism — signs of perforation or peritonitis)
Rectal examination if appropriate: blood on glove; mass or tenderness

Neurological assessment (if botulism or organophosphate poisoning suspected): cranial nerve examination (pupil size and reactivity, ptosis, diplopia, bulbar function), limb tone, reflexes, respiratory rate and effort
Eye examination: jaundice (scleral icterus — hepatitis); pupil size (miosis in organophosphate/Muscarine poisoning; mydriasis in Atropine overdose)
Skin examination: jaundice, rashes (rose spots — typhoid; urticaria — scombroid; petechiae/purpura — HUS/septicaemia), flushing (scombroid)
In children: fontanelle assessment (sunken — dehydration), crying with or without tears, responsiveness

diagnostic_tests.description: Standard test for bacterial food poisoning — stool sent to laboratory for culture on selective media to grow and identify specific bacteria. Sensitivity varies by organism and time of collection — best yield in first 48-72 hours of illness.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify specific bacterial pathogen (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli, Vibrio); guide antibiotic choice
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive culture confirms bacterial aetiology; sensitivity ~50-70% depending on pathogen and timing; report time 48-72 hours

diagnostic_tests.description: Simultaneous PCR testing for multiple bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens from a single stool sample. Much faster (hours vs days) and more sensitive than culture. Tests for 20+ pathogens including bacteria, viruses, and parasites simultaneously.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid and comprehensive aetiological diagnosis; particularly useful for outbreak investigation, immunocompromised patients, and severe illness
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Results in 2-6 hours; sensitivity >90% for most pathogens; includes norovirus, rotavirus, bacteria, and parasites in one panel

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Stool for Ova, Cysts and Parasites (OCP)
diagnostic_tests.description: Microscopic examination of stool for parasites, protozoan cysts, and helminth ova/eggs. Requires three separate stool samples collected on different days (parasites shed intermittently) for optimal sensitivity.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, helminths (roundworms, tapeworms)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Sensitivity for Giardia improved by 3-sample approach (69% → 97%); Cryptosporidium requires special modified acid-fast staining

diagnostic_tests.description: Point-of-care rapid tests for specific pathogens. Results in 15-30 minutes.
examples: Giardia antigen test (ELISA or rapid immunochromatographic) — sensitivity >90%
Clostridium difficile toxin and GDH antigen
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid diagnosis at point-of-care; especially useful for Giardia, Cryptosporidium, C. difficile

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) / Complete Blood Count
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in moderate-severe food poisoning. Leukocytosis with neutrophilia suggests bacterial infection. Leukopenia may occur in typhoid (relative bradycardia + leucopenia is characteristic). Anaemia and thrombocytopenia suggest HUS (haemolytic anaemia + low platelets + elevated creatinine = HUS triad). Eosinophilia may indicate parasitic infection.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess severity of infection; detect HUS; detect typhoid; guide antibiotic decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC >12,000/µL with neutrophilia: bacterial infection; Hb falling + platelets falling + rising creatinine: screen for HUS in STEC illness

diagnostic_tests.description: CRP elevated in bacterial more than viral gastroenteritis. Procalcitonin is more specific for bacterial sepsis — helps distinguish bacterial from viral aetiology and guides antibiotic decisions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess severity; distinguish bacterial from viral; guide antibiotic use
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CRP >50-100 mg/L: serious bacterial infection; Procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL suggests bacterial bacteraemia

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Electrolytes, Renal Function and Blood Glucose
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential for assessing and managing dehydration and complications. Hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia are common in severe diarrhoea. Elevated creatinine and urea indicate dehydration or HUS. Blood glucose: hypoglycaemia in children with poor intake.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess dehydration severity; detect HUS (raised creatinine); detect hyponatraemia/hypokalaemia; guide IV fluid composition
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Creatinine rising + falling platelets + Hb falling = STEC HUS — nephrology urgently; K+ <3.5 mmol/L needs potassium replacement

diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated transaminases (ALT, AST) indicate hepatitis (hepatitis A, E, or CMV) or liver damage (Amanita mushroom poisoning). Markedly elevated bilirubin with raised ALT and dark urine suggests hepatitis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect hepatitis A and E; screen for Amanita mushroom liver failure; assess typhoid hepatitis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ALT >200 U/L with jaundice suggests hepatitis; ALT/AST >1000 U/L in Amanita poisoning indicates fulminant failure — urgently refer for liver transplant assessment

diagnostic_tests.description: Essential when systemic infection (bacteraemia/septicaemia) is suspected. Always take 2-3 sets before starting antibiotics. Takes 48-72 hours for results.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect bacteraemia in: typhoid, invasive Salmonella, Listeria, Campylobacter bacteraemia, septicaemia from bowel infection
diagnostic_tests.indication: High fever (>39°C) with systemic illness; immunocompromised patient with food poisoning; suspected typhoid; Listeria exposure

diagnostic_tests.description: Specific toxin detection in stool or serum.
examples: Clostridium difficile toxin A and B + GDH antigen (in antibiotic-associated diarrhoea)
Shiga toxin (Stx1 and Stx2) for STEC E. coli O157:H7
Botulinum toxin in serum, stool, or food samples (CDC/reference laboratory)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive Shiga toxin: STEC confirmed — DO NOT give antibiotics or loperamide

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Hepatitis A IgM and Hepatitis E IgM Serology
diagnostic_tests.description: IgM antibodies appear early in acute hepatitis A and E infection and confirm recent infection. IgG antibodies indicate past infection or vaccination.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose acute hepatitis A or E foodborne/waterborne hepatitis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive anti-HAV IgM = acute hepatitis A; Positive anti-HEV IgM = acute hepatitis E

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Widal Test / Typhidot / Typhoid Rapid Test
diagnostic_tests.description: Serological tests for typhoid fever. Widal test measures antibodies to Salmonella Typhi O and H antigens. High background seropositivity in endemic areas reduces specificity. Typhidot IgM (anti-OMP IgM) has better performance.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Support diagnosis of typhoid fever in endemic areas when blood culture is not available or negative
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Widal: O titer ≥1:160 and H titer ≥1:160 suggestive; blood culture remains gold standard for typhoid diagnosis

diagnostic_tests.description: Not routinely required for uncomplicated food poisoning. Indicated for: suspected bowel perforation (free air under diaphragm on erect CXR/AXR), amoebic liver abscess (right upper quadrant ultrasound), toxic megacolon (dilated colon >6cm on AXR), intestinal obstruction.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect complications: perforation (free air), amoebic abscess (liver), toxic megacolon, bowel obstruction
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Free air under right hemidiaphragm on erect CXR = bowel perforation (surgical emergency)

diagnostic_tests.description: Detects haematuria and proteinuria — important markers of HUS in STEC infection. Haematuria + proteinuria in a child with bloody diarrhoea = screen urgently for HUS. Also detects urinary tract infection mimicking food poisoning.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect HUS (haematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts in urine); urinary tract infection differential; assess renal involvement

medicines.note: The cornerstone of food poisoning treatment is ORAL REHYDRATION THERAPY — replacing fluids and electrolytes lost through vomiting and diarrhoea. Most uncomplicated food poisoning does not require antibiotics. All medications must be used under medical supervision when indicated. Do NOT take antidiarrhoeal medications with bloody diarrhoea or suspected STEC E. coli infection.
treatment_principles: 1. Oral rehydration is the MOST IMPORTANT treatment for all food poisoning

2. Antibiotics are NOT required for most food poisoning — viruses (no antibiotics), mild bacterial (self-limiting), toxin-mediated (antibiotics not needed). Reserve for severe/systemic bacterial disease.
3. NEVER use antidiarrhoeals (loperamide) for bloody diarrhoea, suspected E. coli O157:H7, or invasive bacterial colitis — increases risk of HUS and toxic megacolon
4. Rest the gut — NPO initially if vomiting; reintroduce clear fluids then soft diet
5. Symptomatic treatment: antiemetics for vomiting, antipyretics for fever
6. Report suspected outbreaks to public health authorities

categories.category_name: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) — MOST IMPORTANT Treatment
categories.purpose: Replace fluids and electrolytes lost through vomiting and diarrhoea. WHO ORS is the single most life-saving intervention for diarrhoeal disease — has saved tens of millions of lives globally since 1970s. Prevents severe dehydration and need for IV fluids in most cases.
categories.who_ors_composition: Sodium 75 mmol/L, Chloride 65 mmol/L, Glucose 75 mmol/L, Potassium 20 mmol/L, Citrate 10 mmol/L; Osmolarity 245 mOsm/L

medicines.name: WHO Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS)
medicines.form: Powder sachet dissolved in 1L of clean water; ready-to-drink solution
medicines.dosage: Adults: 200-400mL after each loose stool; 50-200mL/kg over 4-6 hours for moderate dehydration (assess weight if possible). Children: 5-10mL/kg (small child) after each loose stool; 50-100mL/kg over 4 hours for moderate dehydration; give with a spoon or syringe if vomiting — small amounts every 2-5 minutes
medicines.use_case: ALL food poisoning cases — mild, moderate, and as bridge to IV in severe; the single most important treatment; prevents hospitalisation and death
medicines.mechanism: Glucose co-transport of sodium across intestinal epithelium — sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) remains functional even in diarrhoea, unlike passive sodium absorption
side_effects: Vomiting on first administration (continue — small sips); hypernatraemia if not made up correctly (follow instructions exactly)
Never give to infants without medical guidance if severe vomiting
medicines.who_recommendation: WHO Essential Medicine; first-line treatment for diarrhoeal disease globally; use reduced osmolarity ORS (245 mOsm/L)

medicines.name: Home ORS (Sugar-Salt Solution)
medicines.dosage: 1 level teaspoon of salt + 8 level teaspoons of sugar in 1 litre of clean water; OR add salt to rice water, dal water, or yogurt water
medicines.use_case: When commercial ORS sachets are not immediately available; emergency home rehydration
medicines.note: Less precise than WHO ORS but life-saving when commercial ORS unavailable; safe alternative

medicines.name: Intravenous Fluid Resuscitation (IV Fluids)
medicines.dosage: Moderate dehydration: 20-30 mL/kg Ringer's Lactate IV over 30-60 minutes, then reassess. Severe dehydration/shock: 20 mL/kg IV bolus, repeat if needed. Maintenance: 1.5x normal (150 mL/kg/day children; 2.5-3L/day adults) + ongoing losses replaced
medicines.use_case: Severe dehydration; unable to tolerate oral fluids (persistent vomiting); shock; severe cholera; infants and children with >10% dehydration
medicines.choice: Ringer's Lactate / Hartmann's preferred over plain saline for large volume resuscitation (less hyperchloraemic acidosis); add KCl to fluids once urine output established

categories.purpose: Reduce nausea and vomiting to allow oral rehydration therapy and prevent dehydration. Most important as adjuncts to ORT.

medicines.name: Ondansetron
medicines.form: Tablet, Oral dissolving wafer (ODT), IV/IM Injection
medicines.dosage: Adults: 4-8mg orally or IV 3-4 times daily; Children: 0.15mg/kg per dose (max 8mg) every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: First-line antiemetic for food poisoning-associated vomiting; ODT wafer ideal when patient is vomiting; proven to significantly reduce IV fluid requirements in children with gastroenteritis and vomiting
medicines.mechanism: 5-HT3 receptor antagonist — blocks serotonin-mediated vomiting reflex at CTZ and gut
medicines.evidence: Multiple RCTs in paediatric gastroenteritis: single dose ondansetron reduces vomiting, facilitates ORS intake, and reduces hospitalisation rate by 50%

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dosage: 10mg oral or IV/IM every 8 hours; maximum 5 days
medicines.use_case: Nausea and vomiting in food poisoning; also prokinetic — improves gastric emptying; widely available
side_effects: Acute dystonia and extrapyramidal reactions (especially young women and children) — treat with benztropine or procyclidine
medicines.note: Avoid prolonged use; not recommended in children under 18 years by some guidelines due to dystonia risk; ondansetron preferred in children

medicines.name: Domperidone
medicines.dosage: 10-20mg oral 3 times daily before meals
medicines.use_case: Nausea and vomiting; prokinetic; preferred in children under 18 over metoclopramide (fewer CNS effects as does not cross blood-brain barrier)
side_effects: QT prolongation with high doses (cardiac caution)

medicines.name: Promethazine
medicines.dosage: 25-50mg oral or IM every 6-8 hours
medicines.use_case: Nausea and vomiting in adults; also antihistamine; useful when oral route unavailable
side_effects: Avoid in children <2 years (respiratory depression risk)

categories.purpose: Reduce stool frequency and volume to improve comfort and reduce fluid losses. IMPORTANT CAUTION: Antidiarrhoeals are CONTRAINDICATED in bloody diarrhoea (dysentery), suspected STEC E. coli O157:H7, invasive bacterial colitis, high fever with diarrhoea, and infants under 2 years.
categories.warning: NEVER use loperamide for: bloody diarrhoea, E. coli O157:H7 (increases HUS risk), Shigella, Salmonella with systemic illness, fever >38.5°C — can cause toxic megacolon and delay clearance of pathogens

medicines.name: Loperamide
medicines.dosage: Adults: 4mg initial dose, then 2mg after each loose stool; maximum 16mg/day
medicines.use_case: ONLY for uncomplicated, non-bloody traveller's diarrhoea and watery food poisoning without fever; short-term use only; NOT for dysentery or if STEC suspected
medicines.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor agonist in gut; reduces gut motility and secretions; does not cross blood-brain barrier at therapeutic doses
contraindications: Suspected STEC E. coli O157:H7 — ABSOLUTE contraindication (increases HUS risk)
side_effects: CNS effects at very high doses

medicines.name: Bismuth Subsalicylate
medicines.dosage: Adults: 30mL or 2 tablets every 30-60 minutes; max 8 doses per day
medicines.use_case: Mild to moderate acute diarrhoea and nausea; mild antimicrobial effect; reduces stool frequency; can be used for traveller's diarrhoea
side_effects: Black stools and black tongue (harmless — bismuth salts)
Ringing in ears (tinnitus) — salicylate toxicity with excessive use
contraindications: Children under 12 years (Reye's syndrome risk from salicylate)

categories.purpose: Reduce fever and alleviate abdominal cramps and body aches associated with food poisoning.

medicines.name: Paracetamol / Acetaminophen
medicines.dosage: Adults: 500-1000mg every 4-6 hours (max 4000mg/day; 3000mg if liver disease); Children: 10-15mg/kg every 4-6 hours
medicines.use_case: First-line antipyretic and analgesic for fever and abdominal cramps in food poisoning; safest option
medicines.note: Preferred over NSAIDs when dehydrated — NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow (risk of AKI in dehydration)

medicines.name: Ibuprofen
medicines.dosage: 400-600mg every 6-8 hours with food
medicines.use_case: Fever and pain in food poisoning — use only when adequately rehydrated; take with food
medicines.contraindications_in_food_poisoning: Avoid in: severe dehydration (renal impairment risk), suspected HUS (NSAID nephrotoxicity), GI bleeding, elderly (higher renal AKI risk)

categories.category_name: Antibiotics — Targeted Therapy for Specific Bacterial Food Poisoning
categories.purpose: Antibiotics are NOT required for most food poisoning (viral, toxin-mediated, or mild self-limiting bacterial). Specific antibiotic indications: invasive bacterial disease, systemic illness, immunocompromised patients, at-risk populations, and specific organisms requiring treatment.
categories.note: Antibiotic resistance is a major and growing concern for enteric pathogens — always send stool cultures before antibiotics; follow local resistance data.

medicines.name: Ciprofloxacin
medicines.dosage: 500mg twice daily orally for 3-7 days (Salmonella, Shigella); 500mg twice daily for 3-5 days (Campylobacter — if susceptible); IV: 400mg every 8-12 hours for systemic infection
medicines.use_case: Salmonella (non-typhoidal) in high-risk patients; Shigella dysentery; Campylobacter (increasing resistance — check susceptibility); traveller's diarrhoea; Vibrio cholera; Typhoid (where susceptible)
medicines.mechanism: Fluoroquinolone — inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; bactericidal; broad gram-negative spectrum
medicines.resistance_warning: Ciprofloxacin resistance increasing globally in Campylobacter (>50% in some countries including India) and some Salmonella serotypes — always check local resistance patterns; azithromycin often preferred for Campylobacter
contraindications: Children under 18 years (cartilage effects — use azithromycin instead)
Do NOT use for STEC E. coli O157:H7 (increases HUS risk)

medicines.name: Azithromycin
medicines.dosage: Adults: 500mg once daily for 3-5 days; Children: 10mg/kg once daily for 3-5 days (Campylobacter or Shigella); 500mg once daily for 3 days (traveller's diarrhoea)
medicines.use_case: PREFERRED for Campylobacter (better resistance profile than ciprofloxacin); Shigella; Salmonella in children; traveller's diarrhoea; safe in pregnancy and children
medicines.mechanism: Macrolide antibiotic — inhibits 50S ribosomal subunit; bacteriostatic (bactericidal at high concentrations)

medicines.name: Metronidazole
medicines.dosage: Adults: 400-500mg 3 times daily for 7-10 days (amoebic dysentery, Giardia); 500mg 3 times daily IV (severe amoebic colitis, C. difficile); Children: 35-50mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for Giardia (400mg TDS × 5-7 days); Entamoeba histolytica amoebic dysentery and liver abscess; Clostridium difficile (mild-moderate CDI); anaerobic bacterial infections; Trichomoniasis
medicines.mechanism: Nitroimidazole — enters cells and creates reactive intermediates that damage DNA of anaerobic and protozoan organisms
side_effects: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (severe flushing, vomiting — avoid ALL alcohol during treatment and for 48h after)
medicines.note: Tinidazole 2g single oral dose is as effective as metronidazole course for Giardia and may be better tolerated

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone (IV)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 1-2g IV/IM once daily; Children: 50-100mg/kg/day IV once daily
medicines.use_case: Severe invasive Salmonella (including typhoid and non-typhoidal bacteraemia); Listeria meningitis (with ampicillin); MDRSA (multi-drug resistant Salmonella); Shigella bacteraemia; severe food poisoning requiring parenteral treatment
medicines.note: Preferred IV antibiotic for typhoid fever, severe Salmonella bacteraemia, and when oral route unavailable

medicines.name: Ampicillin + Gentamicin (Combination)
medicines.dosage: Ampicillin 2g IV every 4-6 hours + Gentamicin 5mg/kg IV once daily
medicines.use_case: DRUG OF CHOICE for invasive Listeriosis (bacteraemia, meningitis, pregnancy-associated) — synergistic combination; only treatment with proven efficacy for listeria endocarditis
medicines.monitoring: Gentamicin serum levels and renal function (nephrotoxicity risk)

medicines.name: Vancomycin (Oral)
medicines.dosage: 125mg orally 4 times daily for 10-14 days (CDI)
medicines.use_case: First-line treatment for Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) — antibiotic-associated diarrhoea; oral vancomycin not absorbed systemically — acts locally in colon
medicines.note: NOT used for other food poisoning; IV vancomycin ineffective for CDI (does not reach colon)

medicines.name: Fidaxomicin (Oral)
medicines.dosage: 200mg twice daily for 10 days
medicines.use_case: First-line or preferred treatment for C. difficile — lower recurrence rate than vancomycin; particularly valuable for recurrent CDI
medicines.note: More expensive than vancomycin; preferred by IDSA/SHEA guidelines for first recurrence CDI

medicines.name: Nitazoxanide
medicines.dosage: Adults: 500mg twice daily for 3 days; Children: 7.5-15mg/kg twice daily for 3 days (weight-based)
medicines.use_case: Cryptosporidium parvum (first-line in immunocompetent patients); Giardia lamblia (alternative to metronidazole); broad antiprotozoal and antiviral spectrum; useful in enteric infections where pathogen uncertain
side_effects: Urine and stools may have yellow/green tint (harmless)

medicines.name: Tinidazole
medicines.dosage: Giardia: 2g single dose; Amoebiasis: 2g once daily for 2-3 days
medicines.use_case: Giardia (single-dose — superior adherence vs metronidazole course); Entamoeba histolytica; better tolerated than metronidazole
side_effects: Avoid alcohol during and 72h after use

medicines.name: Heptavalent Botulinum Antitoxin (HBAT)
medicines.dosage: Single IV dose as early as possible (delays in administration reduce efficacy); available through CDC/national public health emergency stockpiles
medicines.use_case: FOODBORNE BOTULISM — MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Must be given as soon as clinical diagnosis suspected — does not reverse existing paralysis but prevents progression. Contact CDC Emergency Operations (USA: 770-488-7100) or national emergency public health authority immediately.
medicines.mechanism: Antibody-based antitoxin neutralises circulating botulinum toxin before it binds to nerve terminals
medicines.note: Report all suspected botulism cases immediately to local/national public health authorities — notifiable disease

categories.purpose: Treat parasitic food and waterborne infections — protozoal and helminthic.

medicines.name: Albendazole
medicines.dosage: Adults: 400mg once daily for 5-7 days (intestinal nematodes); 400mg twice daily for 8-30 days (Trichinella, Toxocara); 400mg twice daily for 3 days (Giardia — alternative)
medicines.use_case: Intestinal roundworms (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris); Trichinella spiralis; Taenia species; alternative for Giardia; treatment of intestinal helminths
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits tubulin polymerisation in parasitic cells — disrupts glucose uptake and causes death of parasites
side_effects: Teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy; contraceptive advice needed

medicines.name: Mebendazole
medicines.dosage: Pinworms: 100mg single dose (repeat after 2 weeks); Roundworms/hookworm/Trichuris: 100mg twice daily for 3 days or 500mg single dose
medicines.use_case: Intestinal nematodes (roundworms, hookworms, pinworms, whipworm); NOT well absorbed — acts locally in gut

medicines.name: Praziquantel
medicines.dosage: Tapeworm (Taenia): 5-10mg/kg single dose; Schistosomiasis: 20mg/kg 2-3 times in one day
medicines.use_case: Tapeworms (Taenia solium, T. saginata); Schistosomiasis; Cysticercosis (with steroid cover)
side_effects: Transient worsening of neurological symptoms in neurocysticercosis (use corticosteroids)

categories.purpose: Restore disrupted gut microbiome after food poisoning and antibiotic use. Reduce duration of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. Multiple RCTs support use in acute infectious diarrhoea.

medicines.name: Saccharomyces boulardii
medicines.dosage: 250-500mg twice daily for 7-14 days
medicines.use_case: Prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea; treatment of acute infectious diarrhoea (reduces duration by ~1 day); particularly effective against C. difficile infection (reduces recurrence)
medicines.mechanism: Non-pathogenic yeast; secretes protease that degrades C. difficile toxin B receptor; immune modulation; restoration of brush border enzymes
medicines.evidence: Cochrane review: reduces duration of acute diarrhoea by 31 hours in children; reduces C. difficile recurrence by 50%

medicines.name: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)
medicines.dosage: 1 capsule (10 billion CFU) twice daily
medicines.use_case: Acute rotavirus diarrhoea in children (reduces duration); antibiotic-associated diarrhoea; traveller's diarrhoea; restores gut microbiome
medicines.evidence: Cochrane review: LGG reduces duration of infectious diarrhoea by average 24 hours

medicines.name: Multi-Strain Probiotics (Lactobacillus + Bifidobacterium combinations)
medicines.dosage: 1-2 capsules/sachets twice daily during and 2 weeks after antibiotic course
medicines.use_case: Prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea; gut microbiome restoration after food poisoning and antibiotics; C. difficile prevention

categories.purpose: WHO recommends zinc supplementation for children with acute diarrhoea in low-to-middle income countries — reduces severity and duration of diarrhoea and prevents recurrence for 2-3 months.

medicines.name: Zinc Sulfate / Zinc Acetate
medicines.dosage: Children <6 months: 10mg once daily for 10-14 days; Children ≥6 months: 20mg once daily for 10-14 days
medicines.use_case: WHO recommends zinc supplementation for ALL children with acute diarrhoea in low-middle income countries; reduces duration by ~25%, reduces volume of diarrhoea by ~30%, and reduces risk of recurrent diarrhoea in following 2-3 months
medicines.mechanism: Zinc is essential for intestinal mucosal healing, immune function, and epithelial barrier integrity; diarrhoea causes significant zinc losses
side_effects: Nausea and vomiting (give with food or ORS)
medicines.authority: WHO and UNICEF recommend zinc + ORS as standard treatment for childhood diarrhoea

categories.purpose: Binds to many toxins and chemicals in the GI tract, preventing absorption. Most effective when given within 1-2 hours of toxic ingestion. Used primarily for chemical poisoning, mushroom poisoning, and some drug overdoses.

medicines.name: Activated Charcoal
medicines.dosage: Adults: 50g as single dose; Children: 1g/kg (max 50g); give as soon as possible within 1-2 hours of ingestion
medicines.use_case: Chemical food poisoning (pesticides, heavy metals); mushroom poisoning (Amanita phalloides — early after ingestion); drug/toxin ingestion
medicines.mechanism: Large surface area adsorbs many toxins and chemicals — binds them in GI tract preventing systemic absorption
medicines.note: NOT effective for: alcohols, iron, lithium, electrolytes, cyanide. Ineffective for bacterial food poisoning (toxin already absorbed)

categories.purpose: Block histamine receptors to treat histamine-mediated symptoms of scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning — urticaria, flushing, GI symptoms. The primary treatment for scombroid poisoning.

medicines.name: Diphenhydramine / Chlorpheniramine (H1 antagonists)
medicines.dosage: Diphenhydramine: 25-50mg orally or IV every 6 hours; Chlorpheniramine: 4mg every 6 hours orally
medicines.use_case: Scombroid fish poisoning (histamine poisoning) — first-line treatment; also urticaria from food allergic reactions

medicines.name: Cetirizine / Loratadine (Non-sedating H1 antagonists)
medicines.dosage: Cetirizine 10mg once daily; Loratadine 10mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Milder scombroid/histamine reactions; less sedation than first-generation antihistamines

medicines.name: Ranitidine / Famotidine (H2 antagonists)
medicines.dosage: Famotidine 20-40mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Used alongside H1 antihistamine for scombroid — H2 blockade addresses additional histamine receptors in GI tract and cardiovascular system
medicines.note: Combination H1+H2 blockade more effective than H1 alone for scombroid poisoning

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Dietary management in food poisoning has three phases: (1) Acute phase — gut rest and oral rehydration; (2) Recovery phase — gradual reintroduction of easily digestible foods; (3) Long-term — gut microbiome restoration with probiotic foods. The traditional BRAT diet (Bananas, Rice, Applesauce, Toast) is a helpful but simplified guide — the goal is foods that are easy to digest, low in fibre and fat, and non-irritating to an inflamed gut. Full dietary recovery typically takes 5-7 days after symptoms resolve.

phase_1_acute.timing: First 4-12 hours — while vomiting and nausea dominate
phase_1_acute.principle: NPO (nil per oral) initially if unable to keep anything down; then small sips
recommended: Start with sips of ORS (5-10mL every 5 minutes if vomiting — gradually increase)
Ice chips to suck if vomiting prevents drinking
Weak herbal teas (ginger tea — anti-nausea; chamomile)
Advance to 30-60mL every 15 minutes when vomiting reduces

phase_2_reintroduction.timing: After 4-12 hours when nausea improves and tolerating fluids
phase_2_reintroduction.principle: BRAT diet or equivalent — bland, easily digestible, low-fat, low-fibre foods that do not stimulate intestinal motility further

recommended_foods.category: BRAT Diet and Equivalent — Core Recovery Foods
recommended_foods.evidence: Traditional and clinically accepted; though evidence for strict BRAT is limited, bland low-fat diet is universally recommended

items.benefit: The 'B' in BRAT. Easily digestible; rich in potassium (replaces electrolytes lost in diarrhoea); pectin (soluble fibre that helps firm stools and slow diarrhoea); natural antacid properties; provides energy when appetite is poor

items.food: Plain boiled white rice (or rice congee/kanji/khichdi)
items.benefit: The 'R' in BRAT. Easily digestible starch; low fibre (does not accelerate transit); rice water (kanji) provides carbohydrates and electrolytes; white rice preferred over brown rice (lower fibre — gentler on inflamed gut); rice congee (watery rice) is ideal initially
items.frequency: Small portions every 2-3 hours as tolerated
items.tip: Cook rice in more water to make congee/kanji/porridge — more digestible and provides hydration

items.benefit: The 'A' in BRAT. Pectin from cooked apples helps firm stools (unlike raw apple); glucose for energy; gentle on gut; easily digestible
items.note: COOKED apple or applesauce — not raw apple (higher fibre in raw form)

items.benefit: The 'T' in BRAT. Simple carbohydrate; easy to digest; helpful for nausea; dry toast absorbs excess gastric acid

items.food: Moong dal khichdi (overcooked rice and lentils)
items.benefit: Indian equivalent of BRAT — excellent post-food poisoning food: easily digestible protein and carbohydrate; soft texture; anti-inflammatory; ghee has antibacterial properties (small amount); warm and comforting; provides energy without overloading gut
items.frequency: Small portions every 3-4 hours from day 2 of illness

items.food: Plain boiled potatoes (no skin, no butter or spices)
items.benefit: Starchy, binding effect; potassium (electrolyte replacement); easily digestible; gentle on GI tract

items.food: Plain boiled pasta or noodles (no sauce)
items.benefit: Simple digestible carbohydrate; low fat and fibre; provides calories during recovery
Hydration; electrolytes (sodium, potassium); easily absorbed; amino acids for gut mucosal healing; warm broth is soothing to inflamed gut; bone broth provides collagen (gut repair)
items.frequency: Multiple times daily during acute and recovery phases
items.tip: Low-sodium homemade broth preferred over commercial (high sodium worsens dehydration)

items.food: Rice water / Kanji (water from boiling rice)
items.benefit: Traditional Indian remedy — very effective: provides glucose, sodium, and starches; helps firm stools; WHO used rice-based ORS in cholera trials (comparable to glucose-based ORS); soothing and easily digested
items.frequency: As much as desired — continuously for hydration

items.benefit: Ginger is the single most evidence-based natural antiemetic — 6-gingerol blocks 5-HT3 receptors (same as ondansetron mechanism); anti-inflammatory; anti-nausea; can abort vomiting when taken at onset
items.frequency: 1-2 cups hourly during nausea; continuing daily throughout recovery
items.preparation: Fresh ginger (1-2 cm piece) in 2 cups boiling water for 5-10 minutes; strain; sip slowly

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — gut microbiome disrupted by food poisoning pathogens and antibiotics. Probiotic foods restore Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations.

items.food: Plain yogurt / Curd (with live active cultures)
items.benefit: Probiotics (Lactobacillus acidophilus, L. bulgaricus, Streptococcus thermophilus) — restore gut flora after food poisoning; reduce duration of diarrhoea; lactase from yogurt bacteria makes it tolerable even in lactose-sensitive patients; protein for recovery
items.frequency: Daily from day 3 of illness (when gut is recovering); continue 4-6 weeks after antibiotic completion
items.note: Choose plain, unsweetened yogurt with 'live cultures' on label; avoid flavoured yogurt (added sugar feeds pathogens)

items.food: Buttermilk / Chaach (diluted yogurt with water and minimal salt)
items.benefit: Excellent Indian probiotic; well-tolerated during recovery; electrolytes; cooling; probiotics; easier to digest than solid yogurt; traditional post-diarrhoea remedy with strong logic

items.food: Idli and dosa (fermented rice and lentil dishes — without sambar initially)
items.benefit: Fermented foods with natural probiotics; easily digestible soft texture (especially idli); provide carbohydrate and protein without heavy fat; ideal recovery foods in South Indian diet

Natural electrolyte drink — potassium (600mg/cup), sodium, magnesium, glucose; near-isotonic; excellent natural ORS-like fluid; soothing; well-tolerated during nausea; superior to plain water for rehydration
items.frequency: 1-2 cups daily during and after illness

items.benefit: WHO-formulated electrolyte replacement — precisely calibrated sodium-glucose-potassium mixture; more effective than plain water for rehydration (glucose co-transport of sodium)

items.food: Diluted apple juice or orange juice (very diluted — 1:1 with water)
items.benefit: Potassium; glucose; gentle flavour encourages fluid intake in children who refuse plain water; avoid full-strength juice (high sugar — can worsen osmotic diarrhoea)
Complete protein; easily digestible; zinc (gut healing); Vitamin B12; soft texture; can reintroduce from day 3 of recovery

items.food: Steamed or boiled fish (lean white fish)
items.benefit: High-quality lean protein; easily digestible; omega-3 anti-inflammatory; minimal fat; gentle on recovering gut

items.food: Biscuits and crackers (plain — cream crackers, water biscuits)
items.benefit: Simple digestible carbohydrate; low fat; help with nausea; provide energy when appetite is poor

foods_to_avoid.reason: Food poisoning pathogens (particularly Rotavirus, Giardia, Cryptosporidium) temporarily reduce lactase enzyme in small intestinal brush border — causing secondary lactose intolerance. Drinking milk in the acute phase causes osmotic diarrhoea (bloating, cramping, more diarrhoea).
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid for 3-7 days; reintroduce plain yogurt first (lactase-producing bacteria make it tolerable); then milk gradually
foods_to_avoid.exception: Plain yogurt with live cultures is an EXCEPTION — tolerated even with lactose intolerance because the bacteria produce lactase; beneficial probiotic effect

foods_to_avoid.reason: High fat content delays gastric emptying and stimulates intestinal motility — worsening diarrhoea; difficult to digest with inflamed intestinal mucosa; increases nausea
examples: Ghee and butter in large quantities
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid for 5-7 days; reintroduce very gradually

foods_to_avoid.reason: Capsaicin irritates already-inflamed intestinal mucosa; activates TRPV1 receptors in gut increasing motility and secretion — worsening diarrhoea and abdominal cramps; prolongs gut inflammation

Insoluble fibre accelerates intestinal transit — worsening diarrhoea in acute phase; difficult to digest with inflamed gut. Soluble fibre (pectin from bananas and cooked apples) actually helps firm stools.
examples: Brown rice and whole wheat pasta
foods_to_avoid.note: Gradually reintroduce cooked vegetables from day 4-5; full fibre diet from week 2
foods_to_avoid.exception: Soluble fibre in bananas and cooked apples is beneficial — it firms stools

foods_to_avoid.reason: Severely irritates already-inflamed intestinal mucosa; causes vasodilation worsening diarrhoea; dehydrating (diuretic effect worsens fluid losses); ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION with metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction); impairs immune function slowing recovery; toxic to inflamed liver (especially hepatitis A/E)
foods_to_avoid.duration: Complete abstinence during illness and treatment; minimum 48 hours after completing metronidazole; 4 weeks with hepatitis A/E

foods_to_avoid.reason: High osmolarity of sugary drinks causes osmotic diarrhoea (the concentrated sugar draws water into the gut — worsening fluid losses); glucose feeds pathogenic bacteria; spikes then crashes blood sugar
foods_to_avoid.note: ORS sachets contain a precise amount of glucose that is beneficial for sodium co-transport — do NOT add extra sugar to ORS

foods_to_avoid.reason: Caffeine is a GI stimulant — increases intestinal motility and secretion, worsening diarrhoea; diuretic effect worsens dehydration; can worsen nausea; disrupts sleep needed for recovery
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid during acute illness; reintroduce weak tea cautiously after 3-4 days

foods_to_avoid.reason: During recovery the gut is vulnerable to additional pathogens; raw foods during recovery can introduce new foodborne pathogens; immune system temporarily impaired
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid completely until full recovery (7-10 days)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Large portions overload a compromised digestive system — overwhelm reduced gastric acid production, impaired intestinal enzyme function, and damaged mucosal absorptive capacity
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Small, frequent meals (5-6 small portions per day) preferred over 3 large meals for 7-10 days during recovery

sample_meal_plan.note: This graduated recovery plan assumes mild-moderate food poisoning improving after first 12-24 hours. Adjust based on individual symptoms and recovery speed. Advance only if previous step tolerated. Every patient is different.
sample_meal_plan.day_0_acute_phase: NPO (nothing by mouth) while actively vomiting → sips of ORS or ice chips → small sips cold water (30-60mL every 5-15 minutes) → ginger tea sips → advance to step 2 when nausea reduces
sample_meal_plan.day_1: ORS sachets (main fluid); Rice water / kanji; Plain white rice congee (watery, no spice, no salt); Weak ginger tea; Banana (half, if tolerated); Clear chicken broth; Coconut water
sample_meal_plan.day_2: ORS; Plain boiled rice (slightly thicker congee); Half banana; Plain toast; Boiled potato (no skin, no butter); Stewed apple; Moong dal soup; Chamomile/ginger herbal tea; Plain water
sample_meal_plan.day_3_to_4: Plain boiled rice with moong dal khichdi; 1 boiled egg (scrambled); Plain yogurt/curd (probiotic); Ripe banana; Cream crackers; Diluted apple juice; Boiled carrot (well cooked); Plain broth
sample_meal_plan.day_5_to_7: Normal soft foods gradually reintroduced: boiled rice or plain chapati + dal; Steamed or boiled fish; Yogurt; Soft cooked vegetables (without strong spices); Oatmeal porridge; Avoid raw vegetables, fried foods, spicy dishes, and dairy (except yogurt)
sample_meal_plan.week_2_onwards: Normal balanced diet gradually resumed; reintroduce fibre, cooked then raw vegetables; probiotics daily (yogurt/kefir); maintain good hydration; avoid alcohol for 2-4 weeks

special_dietary_notes: ORS sachets are far superior to plain water or sports drinks for rehydration — they use glucose-sodium co-transport to actively replace electrolytes; make up exactly as directed on packet (do not add extra sugar or dilute)
Rice water (kanji) and coconut water are excellent traditional Indian rehydration fluids with clinical evidence — use freely
NEVER force eat if nauseated — fluid replacement is priority over food for first 24 hours; the body tolerates days without food much better than hours without fluids

Probiotics (yogurt with live cultures, Saccharomyces boulardii supplements) from day 3 of illness and throughout antibiotic course significantly reduce recovery time and prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhoea
Children with food poisoning: give ORS in small amounts CONTINUOUSLY (5-10mL every 2-5 min); never restrict fluids; offer favourite clear fluids (diluted juice, coconut water) to encourage intake
Return to normal diet as quickly as tolerated — prolonged restrictive diets are not recommended; gradual return to normal eating is better than prolonged BRAT diet restriction
Zinc 20mg daily for 10-14 days in children under 5 years — WHO recommendation; reduces duration and prevents recurrence

food_safety_and_prevention.overview: The vast majority of food poisoning cases are preventable through proper food safety practices. The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food provide a practical framework for food safety in homes and food service settings.

measures: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water for ≥20 seconds: before handling food, after handling raw meat/poultry/seafood, after toilet use, after changing nappies, after touching animals or pets, after touching rubbish/waste
Wash and sanitise all food preparation surfaces and equipment before and after use
Wash utensils, chopping boards, and kitchen equipment with hot soapy water after contact with raw meat
Protect food preparation areas from insects, pets, and other animals
Ensure kitchen cloths and sponges are replaced frequently — they harbour bacteria
Keep raw meat, poultry, and seafood separate from ready-to-eat foods — in shopping bag, during refrigeration, and during preparation
Use separate chopping boards and utensils for raw meat and for vegetables/cooked foods
Store raw meat/poultry on the bottom shelf of refrigerator to prevent drip contamination onto foods below
Do not wash raw chicken — this spreads Campylobacter around the sink and surfaces; cooking to correct temperature kills it more effectively
Never place cooked food on plates or surfaces that had raw meat on them
Cook poultry to internal temperature ≥75°C throughout (no pink flesh; juices run clear)
Cook ground/minced meat (burgers, meatballs) to ≥71°C throughout — cannot rely on colour (no pink)
Cook eggs until yolk and white are firm (or to at least 71°C)
Bring soups and stews to boil (≥100°C) during reheating
Use a food thermometer for precise temperature checking
Defrost frozen food in refrigerator or under cold running water — never at room temperature
Reheat leftovers only ONCE to ≥75°C throughout; never reheat multiple times
Refrigerate cooked food within 1 hour (2 hours maximum) of cooking — do not leave at room temperature
Set refrigerator to ≤4°C (40°F) and freezer to ≤-18°C (0°F)
Do not overload refrigerator — air must circulate to maintain temperature
Thaw frozen foods only in refrigerator, in microwave (use immediately), or under cold running water
Keep hot food hot (≥63°C) and cold food cold (≤4°C) during service
Never leave buffet food at room temperature for more than 2 hours (1 hour if ambient temperature >30°C)
Cool large batches of hot food rapidly using ice baths before refrigerating — do not place steaming hot food in refrigerator (raises internal temperature)

who_five_keys.key: 5. USE SAFE WATER AND RAW MATERIALS
measures: Use safe water (boiled, filtered, or bottled) — especially for drinking and washing salads when water quality uncertain
Wash all fresh fruits and vegetables thoroughly under running clean water before consumption
Choose pasteurised milk, dairy products, and juices over unpasteurised
Check expiry dates and discard out-of-date food
Do not use damaged, dented, bulging, or corroded cans (possible Botulinum contamination)
Check for signs of spoilage: unusual odour, colour, mould — if in doubt, throw it out
When travelling, follow 'boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it' principle for food and water safety

home_hygiene_measures: Wash hands with soap for ≥20 seconds at key times — before eating, after toilet use, after handling raw food, after contact with sick people
Use alcohol-based hand sanitizer (≥60% alcohol) when soap unavailable
Disinfect kitchen surfaces with dilute bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per gallon of water) or commercial disinfectant after food preparation
Wash dishcloths and tea towels frequently at 60°C — they are major reservoirs of bacteria and norovirus
