Replace kitchen sponges regularly — clean in dishwasher at high temperature; microwaving damp sponge for 2 minutes kills most bacteria
Childproof measures: store cleaning chemicals away from food preparation areas
Sick household members: use separate bathroom if possible; exclude from food preparation
Wash hands after contact with any sick person — norovirus is extremely contagious

isolation_and_infection_control.return_to_work_school: Stay home for 48 hours after the LAST episode of diarrhoea or vomiting
isolation_and_infection_control.food_handlers: Food handlers and healthcare workers: 48 hours symptom-free before returning to work; some pathogens (Typhoid, Salmonella) require negative stool cultures before returning

exclusion_periods.salmonella_non_typhoidal: 48 hours after last symptoms (longer exclusion for food handlers)
exclusion_periods.typhoid: Until negative stool cultures confirmed (can be months-long carrier)
exclusion_periods.hepatitis_A: 1 week after onset of jaundice or dark urine
exclusion_periods.shigella: 48 hours after last symptoms; negative stool culture for food handlers

isolation_and_infection_control.contact_tracing: If outbreak suspected (multiple people affected after same food/event) — contact local/district public health or Environmental Health Office for outbreak investigation and food safety enforcement

travel_food_safety.principle: Boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it
measures: Drink only bottled, boiled, or purified water — avoid tap water, ice, and drinks with ice in high-risk destinations
Eat only hot freshly cooked food — avoid food that has been sitting at room temperature
Eat fruit you can peel yourself — avoid pre-peeled or pre-cut fruit
Avoid raw shellfish, raw vegetables, and salads in high-risk areas
Be cautious with street food — choose busy stalls with high turnover where food is cooked fresh
Carry oral rehydration sachets, probiotics, and bismuth subsalicylate for traveller's diarrhoea prevention
Consider typhoid vaccine and hepatitis A vaccine before travel to endemic areas
Travellers' diarrhoea prophylaxis: bismuth subsalicylate reduces risk by 65%; antibiotics (rifaximin, ciprofloxacin) for high-risk travellers under medical advice

post_illness_recovery_lifestyle: Rest adequately — the immune system requires energy; avoid strenuous activity for 48-72 hours after symptoms resolve
Maintain good hydration — drink at least 2-2.5 litres daily for 1-2 weeks after illness
Continue probiotics (yogurt, kefir, or supplements) for 4-6 weeks after illness and throughout antibiotic course
Gradually reintroduce normal diet over 7-10 days — do not rush
Avoid alcohol for 2-4 weeks post-illness (liver recovery time, especially hepatitis A/E)
Return to exercise cautiously — start with walking; avoid intense exercise until energy levels normalised
Monitor for post-infectious complications: persistent loose stools >4 weeks (post-infectious IBS), joint pain (reactive arthritis), fatigue (hepatitis recovery)
Seek GP review if not fully recovered at 2-4 weeks — exclude parasitic infection or post-infectious IBS

food_poisoning_monitoring_plan.note: Most food poisoning is self-limiting and resolves with home management. This monitoring guide helps determine when home care is sufficient and when medical attention is urgently needed.

green_zone.status: Mild — Safe to Manage at Home
green_zone.criteria: Vomiting fewer than 5 times in 24 hours; diarrhoea fewer than 8 times in 24 hours; NO blood in stool; able to keep down small sips of ORS; temperature <38.5°C; alert and oriented; adequate urine output (pale yellow urine); not in at-risk group (young infant, elderly, pregnant, immunocompromised)
green_zone.action: Home management with ORS sachets, rest, and BRAT diet. Monitor symptoms every 2-4 hours. Advance oral fluids as tolerated. Antiemetics if vomiting prevents ORS intake. Should show improvement within 24-48 hours. If not improving or worsening — move to yellow zone.

yellow_zone.status: Moderate — Seek Medical Attention Within Hours
yellow_zone.criteria: Vomiting preventing ORS intake; diarrhoea >8-10 times per day; signs of moderate dehydration (very dry mouth, decreased urine output, dizziness on standing); fever 38.5-39°C; illness in high-risk person (child <2 years, elderly >65, pregnancy, immunocompromised, diabetes); no improvement after 24-48 hours of home management; mucus in stool; blood-tinged stool
yellow_zone.action: Contact GP or attend urgent care/walk-in clinic within hours. Blood tests and stool samples likely required. IV fluids may be needed. Antiemetics prescribed. Consider antibiotic based on clinical assessment. Closely monitor for worsening — admission may be required.

red_zone.status: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Go to Emergency Department Immediately
criteria_immediate: Frank blood in stool (bright red or dark/tarry) — possible dysentery, HUS, or invasive infection
Signs of severe dehydration: no urination >8-12 hours, confusion or altered consciousness, rapid weak pulse, cold clammy hands, sunken eyes, skin not returning after gentle pinch
High fever >39.5°C with abdominal rigidity or guarding
Neurological symptoms: double vision, drooping eyelid (ptosis), difficulty swallowing, slurred speech, progressive muscle weakness — POSSIBLE BOTULISM — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES
Signs of septic shock: low blood pressure, rapid weak pulse, confusion, cold pale extremities
In a child: no wet nappy for 8+ hours, no tears when crying, unable to wake or very lethargic, purple or mottled skin
Jaundice (yellow eyes or skin) — possible hepatitis or Amanita mushroom liver failure
Inability to swallow fluids or saliva — possible peritonitis or serious systemic illness
Severe constant abdominal pain with board-like rigidity — possible bowel perforation
Pregnant woman with food poisoning symptoms after eating at-risk foods (soft cheese, deli meat, smoked fish) — possible Listeria
red_zone.action: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112/999/911) or get to emergency department immediately. Do NOT attempt home management for these features. If botulism suspected — call emergency services AND national public health emergency line immediately.

complications.description: The most common and immediately dangerous complication of food poisoning — especially in infants, young children, elderly, and those with severe vomiting and diarrhoea. Leads to hypovolaemia, acute kidney injury, and cardiovascular collapse. Hypokalaemia from diarrhoea can cause cardiac arrhythmias. Hyponatraemia (from giving plain water without electrolytes) causes cerebral oedema — paradoxically dangerous in children.
complications.management: ORS (oral rehydration); IV Ringer's Lactate for severe dehydration/shock; electrolyte replacement (especially potassium); monitoring of urine output and electrolytes

complications.description: Life-threatening triad: (1) Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (red blood cell destruction), (2) Thrombocytopenia (low platelets), and (3) Acute renal failure (oliguria, rising creatinine). Occurs in 5-10% of children infected with STEC (Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7). Shiga toxin damages endothelial cells in kidney glomeruli and other organs.
complications.warning_signs: Decreased urine output 3-5 days into E. coli illness; pallor, unusual fatigue, bruising or petechiae after diarrhoea resolves
complications.severity: Life-threatening — 3-5% mortality; 25-30% develop long-term renal impairment
complications.management: Supportive — IV fluids and monitoring; dialysis if severe AKI; red blood cell transfusion for severe anaemia; platelet transfusion generally avoided (worsens thrombosis); NO antibiotics; NO loperamide; eculizumab (complement inhibitor) in severe cases
complications.critical_note: DO NOT GIVE ANTIBIOTICS or LOPERAMIDE for STEC O157:H7 — both increase HUS risk by increasing Shiga toxin release

complications.description: Bacterial invasion of the bloodstream from the GI tract — particularly Salmonella, Listeria, Campylobacter, Shigella, and Yersinia. Presents as high fever, rigors, severe illness beyond the GI tract, and systemic inflammatory response. Can lead to septic shock, multi-organ failure, and death.
complications.risk_groups: Immunocompromised patients, elderly, infants, patients with underlying chronic disease
complications.management: IV antibiotics (after blood cultures); ICU support if septic shock; vasopressors if hypotensive

complications.description: Sterile inflammatory arthritis developing 1-4 weeks after gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection. Predominantly affects large joints of lower limbs (knees, ankles). Classic Reiter's syndrome triad: arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'). Triggered by: Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia, Cryptosporidium, Giardia.
complications.severity: Moderate; usually self-limiting (weeks to months) but can become chronic
complications.management: NSAIDs for pain; physiotherapy; DMARDs (sulfasalazine) for chronic reactive arthritis

complications.description: Acute post-infectious autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy causing ascending flaccid paralysis. Campylobacter jejuni is the MOST COMMON identified antecedent infection (20-40% of GBS cases follow Campylobacter gastroenteritis). Molecular mimicry — antibodies against Campylobacter lipo-oligosaccharides cross-react with gangliosides in peripheral nerves.
complications.severity: Severe — can cause respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support; 5% mortality; 20% residual weakness
complications.timing: Neurological symptoms 2-6 weeks after diarrhoea episode
complications.warning_signs: Progressive ascending weakness starting in legs, sensory disturbances, facial weakness, difficulty breathing
complications.management: IV immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis; ICU respiratory monitoring; rehabilitation

complications.description: Persistent alteration in bowel habit and abdominal discomfort lasting more than 3 months after an episode of acute infectious gastroenteritis. Affects 5-10% of patients after food poisoning. Mechanisms include persistent low-grade mucosal inflammation, altered gut microbiome, and changed gut motility and sensory function.
complications.risk_factors: Prolonged/severe initial illness, female sex, stress during illness, treatment with antibiotics
complications.severity: Moderate; chronic; significantly affects quality of life
complications.management: Dietary modification; probiotics; antispasmodics; FODMAP diet; psychological support (CBT for IBS)

complications.description: Listeria monocytogenes has a predilection for the central nervous system — can cause meningitis (neck stiffness, photophobia, fever, headache), rhombencephalitis (brainstem inflammation), and brain abscess. Occurs in elderly, immunocompromised, and neonates. High mortality (20-30%).
complications.management: IV ampicillin + gentamicin; add trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole if penicillin allergy; prolonged IV therapy (3-6 weeks for CNS infection)

complications.complication: Fulminant Hepatic Failure (Mushroom Poisoning / Hepatitis A/E)
complications.description: Life-threatening acute liver failure from: Amanita phalloides mushroom poisoning (amatoxins cause direct hepatocellular necrosis); or severe acute hepatitis A/E (rare in young adults; case fatality 1.8% in >50 year olds with HAV; 20-25% in pregnant women with HEV).
complications.management: Liver transplant assessment; N-acetylcysteine; IV silibinin (for Amanita); supportive ICU care

complications.description: Extraintestinal complication of Entamoeba histolytica — amoebae invade through intestinal wall into portal circulation and form abscess in liver (usually right lobe). Presents weeks to months after GI infection with fever, right upper quadrant pain, tender hepatomegaly. May be present without prior diarrhoea.
complications.management: Metronidazole 750mg TDS for 10-14 days; followed by luminal agent; image-guided aspiration if large abscess or no response to medication

complications.description: Botulinum toxin causes progressive descending flaccid paralysis — starting from cranial nerves (ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia) then descending to respiratory muscles. Without respiratory support, botulism causes death from respiratory failure.
complications.management: Heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (HBAT) as early as possible; ICU respiratory monitoring; mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure; prolonged ICU stay (weeks to months); physical rehabilitation

key_points: Children under 5 years are at highest risk for severe food poisoning and death from dehydration

Signs of dehydration in children are different from adults — assess: sunken fontanelle (infants), sunken eyes, no tears when crying, dry mouth, no wet nappy in 6+ hours, very lethargic or abnormally irritable
Dehydration develops much faster in children (hours) than adults — immediate ORS is critical
Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe diarrhoea in unvaccinated children — rotavirus vaccine has dramatically reduced childhood hospitalisation for gastroenteritis
NEVER withhold ORS in vomiting children — give 5-10mL every 2-5 minutes by spoon or syringe; even if vomiting, small frequent sips are absorbed
Ondansetron single dose in children with vomiting is evidence-based and safe — reduces hospitalisation significantly
Zinc supplementation (10-20mg/day for 10-14 days) — WHO recommendation for children <5 with acute diarrhoea
Do NOT give antidiarrhoeal medications (loperamide) to children under 2 years
Do NOT give plain water alone to dehydrated children — use ORS (plain water dilutes electrolytes dangerously in infants)
Return to school: 48 hours after last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting
Children in daycare/nursery settings are high-risk — notify staff of illness for outbreak control
Breastfeeding should CONTINUE during food poisoning — breastmilk provides antibodies, hydration, and immune support; do not stop breastfeeding

Listeria monocytogenes causes particularly severe illness in pregnancy — even mild flu-like symptoms in pregnancy after eating high-risk foods (soft cheese, deli meats, smoked fish, pre-packaged salads, pâté) warrant URGENT medical assessment and empirical IV ampicillin
Listeria: low incidence but 13x higher risk in pregnancy; causes miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth, and neonatal meningitis; 20% case fatality in pregnancy
Hepatitis E: 20-25% case fatality in 3rd trimester; WASH hands after contact with animals; avoid undercooked pork and wild game
Toxoplasma: from raw/undercooked meat, unwashed vegetables, cat faeces; causes foetal abnormalities, chorioretinitis, and miscarriage — avoid raw meat and change cat litter with gloves
Salmonella and Campylobacter: may cause bacteraemia in pregnancy; treat with azithromycin (ciprofloxacin safe in 2nd and 3rd trimester for severe disease)
Dehydration in pregnancy: severe dehydration triggers preterm contractions — ensure adequate IV fluid replacement early
Safe antibiotics in pregnancy: Amoxicillin, Azithromycin, Cephalosporins, Ampicillin (for Listeria); AVOID: Ciprofloxacin (1st trimester), Metronidazole (1st trimester), Tetracyclines
Hepatitis A and typhoid vaccination recommended BEFORE travel to endemic areas if planning pregnancy
Report any suspected Listeria exposure or illness in pregnancy IMMEDIATELY to obstetrician and infectious disease team
listeria_high_risk_foods_avoid: Soft and semi-soft cheeses (brie, camembert, blue cheese, feta, ricotta)
Ready-to-eat deli meats, hot dogs, pâté (unless reheated until steaming)

key_points: Adults over 65 are at high risk for severe food poisoning complications due to: reduced gastric acid (less protective barrier), impaired immune response, multiple comorbidities, polypharmacy, reduced thirst sensation leading to underhydration
Dehydration signs may be less obvious in elderly — check urine output, mental status changes, and blood pressure
Salmonella and Listeria more likely to cause bacteraemia in elderly — lower threshold for blood cultures and antibiotics
Medications: PPIs reduce gastric acid barrier (increase susceptibility); immunosuppressants reduce ability to fight infection; anticoagulants increase bleeding risk with dysentery
Hospitalisation threshold should be lower for elderly food poisoning — even moderate dehydration is harder to manage at home
Post-infectious IBS and reactive arthritis are more debilitating in elderly
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination does not protect against food poisoning; typhoid and Hep A vaccines recommended before travel
HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200), organ transplant recipients, chemotherapy patients, patients on high-dose steroids or biologics are at dramatically higher risk for severe, invasive, and prolonged food poisoning

Cryptosporidium: causes chronic, severe, potentially life-threatening watery diarrhoea in AIDS patients (CD4 <50) — no reliable antibiotic treatment; nitazoxanide has limited benefit; only effective treatment is immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy
Salmonella and Campylobacter: much higher rates of bacteraemia; consider empirical antibiotics for all immunocompromised patients with bacterial food poisoning
Listeria: 300x higher risk in immunocompromised vs healthy adults; empirical IV ampicillin for any febrile illness after eating high-risk foods in immunocompromised patients
CMV gastritis and enteritis: consider in severe immunosuppressed patients with unexplained GI symptoms
Food safety counselling is CRITICAL for immunocompromised patients — strict avoidance of all raw/undercooked foods, raw shellfish, soft cheeses, deli meats, raw sprouts
Report all significant food poisoning in immunocompromised patients to infectious disease team

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Vi polysaccharide injectable: single dose; booster every 2-3 years. Ty21a oral: 4 capsules over 8 days; booster every 5 years (not for immunocompromised)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Salmonella Typhi (typhoid fever) is a major foodborne and waterborne disease globally — especially in South Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh), Southeast Asia, and Sub-Saharan Africa. Vaccination recommended before travel to endemic areas and for food handlers in endemic regions.
vaccinations_recommended.effectiveness: 50-80% protective efficacy; reduces severity even if infection occurs
vaccinations_recommended.note: Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) increasingly available — single dose; higher efficacy; use in children ≥6 months and adults

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is transmitted through contaminated food and water — a major foodborne pathogen especially in areas with poor sanitation. Shellfish, salads, and raw produce contaminated by infected food handlers are primary vehicles. Vaccination recommended for: travellers to endemic areas, food handlers, healthcare workers, HIV-positive individuals, and people with chronic liver disease
vaccinations_recommended.effectiveness: >95% protective efficacy after 2 doses; lifelong protection

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe diarrhoea and dehydration in children under 5 worldwide — responsible for over 200,000 deaths annually. Rotavirus vaccine has dramatically reduced rotavirus-related hospitalisations by 85-90% in countries with universal vaccination (e.g., USA, UK, India — NTAGI recommended).
vaccinations_recommended.target: All infants from 6 weeks of age; recommended in India under Universal Immunisation Programme

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2 doses given 1-6 weeks apart; booster every 2 years; recommended 1 week before travel

vaccinations_recommended.effectiveness: 65-85% protective efficacy against cholera for 2 years

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Practical combined travel vaccine; both diseases transmitted through contaminated food and water in developing countries; single injection improves compliance for travellers
vaccinations_recommended.note: Requires hepatitis A booster at 6-18 months for lifelong protection

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Not directly protective against food poisoning bacteria. However, influenza illness can severely immunocompromise patients making them more susceptible to bacterial food poisoning complications. Food handlers should be vaccinated to prevent workplace spread of respiratory and potentially foodborne illness.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is food poisoning and how is it different from a stomach bug?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Food poisoning is illness caused specifically by consuming contaminated food or drink — whether contaminated with bacteria (Salmonella, Campylobacter), viruses (norovirus, rotavirus), parasites (Giardia, Entamoeba), or toxins (Staph enterotoxin, Botulinum toxin). A 'stomach bug' (gastroenteritis) is a broader term — it includes food poisoning but also includes illnesses spread person-to-person (such as norovirus spread from touching infected surfaces). In practice there is significant overlap — norovirus is the most common cause of both food poisoning outbreaks and 'stomach bugs'. The key feature of food poisoning is a clear link to a specific food or meal.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How quickly does food poisoning start after eating contaminated food?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Timing depends entirely on the causative agent: (1) Very fast (1-6 hours): Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin or Bacillus cereus emetic toxin — pre-formed toxin in food; (2) 6-24 hours: Clostridium perfringens, Bacillus cereus diarrhoeal toxin, Vibrio; (3) 12-72 hours: Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli, Norovirus; (4) 1-3 weeks: Giardia, Hepatitis A, Typhoid; (5) Weeks to months: Entamoeba. Very short onset (under 6 hours) strongly suggests toxin already in food rather than bacterial infection.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the most important treatment for food poisoning?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) with WHO-formulated ORS sachets is the single most important and life-saving treatment for food poisoning. ORS replaces fluids and electrolytes lost through vomiting and diarrhoea and has saved tens of millions of lives globally. It is far more effective than plain water alone because it uses the sodium-glucose co-transport mechanism that remains functional even in severe diarrhoea. Most mild to moderate food poisoning resolves with rest, ORS, and bland diet — without antibiotics.

frequently_asked_questions.question: When should I take antibiotics for food poisoning?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Most food poisoning does NOT require antibiotics. Antibiotics are NOT helpful for: viral food poisoning (norovirus, rotavirus, hepatitis A), toxin-mediated food poisoning (Staph, B. cereus, Botulinum), mild self-limiting bacterial gastroenteritis, or suspected STEC E. coli O157:H7 (antibiotics actually INCREASE risk of HUS). Antibiotics ARE indicated for: typhoid fever, invasive Salmonella bacteraemia, severe Campylobacter or Shigella, Giardia and Entamoeba (metronidazole), Listeria (IV ampicillin), severe or immunocompromised patients, and Cholera. Always based on clinical assessment by a doctor.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Should I use loperamide (Imodium) to stop diarrhoea?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Loperamide (Imodium) CAN be used for mild, uncomplicated watery diarrhoea in adults (e.g., traveller's diarrhoea). However, it is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in: bloody diarrhoea, suspected E. coli O157:H7 (massively increases HUS risk), high fever with diarrhoea, Shigella or invasive bacterial diarrhoea, and children under 2 years. Diarrhoea is the body's way of expelling pathogens and toxins — stopping it prematurely can cause dangerous bacterial retention, toxic megacolon, or HUS. When in doubt, do not use loperamide — see a doctor.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (HUS) and how does it happen?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: HUS is a life-threatening complication that occurs in 5-10% of children infected with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 (STEC). It presents 5-10 days after bloody diarrhoea with: anaemia (pale, tired), low platelets (bruising), and acute kidney failure (reduced urine output). Shiga toxin damages small blood vessels in the kidneys and other organs. Treatment is entirely supportive — no antibiotics (increase HUS risk), no loperamide. Early recognition is crucial: any child with bloody diarrhoea who develops pallor, reduced urine output, or bruising needs emergency evaluation. HUS kills 3-5% and causes long-term kidney disease in 25-30%.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What foods should I avoid after food poisoning?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Avoid for the first 3-7 days: dairy products (except plain yogurt), fatty and fried foods, spicy foods, raw vegetables and salads, high-fibre foods, alcohol (especially with metronidazole), caffeine, full-strength fruit juices, and sugary beverages. Gradually reintroduce these over 7-10 days as the gut recovers. Focus on: ORS, BRAT diet (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast), clear broths, rice water (kanji), coconut water, plain yogurt (probiotic), and plain boiled easy-to-digest foods.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is botulism and why is it so dangerous?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Botulism is a life-threatening illness caused by botulinum toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum in improperly preserved/canned foods, especially home-preserved low-acid vegetables, fermented products, and honey (infant botulism). The toxin causes progressive descending paralysis — starting with ptosis (drooping eyelid), double vision, difficulty swallowing and speaking, then progressing to arm weakness, leg weakness, and finally respiratory muscle paralysis causing death from asphyxiation. It is treated with heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (HBAT) and ICU respiratory support. Warning signs: double vision or drooping eyelid 12-72 hours after eating — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How do I know if I have Giardia rather than a regular stomach bug?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Giardia infection has characteristic features distinguishing it from typical food poisoning: (1) Duration — persists for weeks to months without treatment (not the usual 24-48 hours); (2) Greasy, foul-smelling, floating stools (steatorrhoea) from fat malabsorption; (3) Excessive flatulence and sulphur/egg burps; (4) Bloating and abdominal distension; (5) NO blood in stool; (6) Weight loss over weeks; (7) History of travel or drinking untreated water. Diagnosis requires stool antigen test or stool microscopy (3 separate samples). Treatment: metronidazole 400mg TDS for 7 days or tinidazole 2g single dose.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can food poisoning be prevented?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — approximately 90% of food poisoning cases are preventable with proper food safety. The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food are: (1) Keep clean — wash hands thoroughly before cooking and after toilet; (2) Separate raw and cooked foods — different chopping boards, separate storage; (3) Cook thoroughly — use a food thermometer; poultry to 75°C; (4) Keep at safe temperatures — refrigerate within 1-2 hours of cooking; (5) Use safe water and raw materials — wash produce, use pasteurised dairy, drink treated water. Vaccinate children against rotavirus. Typhoid and hepatitis A vaccines before travel to endemic areas.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How long should I stay off work after food poisoning?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Most people can return to work 24-48 hours after symptoms resolve. However, if you work as a food handler, healthcare worker, or in a childcare setting, you should remain off for 48 hours AFTER the LAST episode of diarrhoea or vomiting. For specific pathogens: typhoid and Salmonella typhi (food handlers need negative stool cultures), hepatitis A (1 week after jaundice onset), and norovirus (48 hours after last symptoms — highly contagious). Always follow occupational health guidance for your workplace.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the BRAT diet and is it still recommended?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: BRAT stands for Bananas, Rice, Applesauce (stewed), and Toast — a traditional bland, low-fibre, easy-to-digest diet for gastroenteritis recovery. It remains a reasonable starting point but is considered overly restrictive on its own. Current guidelines recommend a broader bland diet: clear fluids and ORS first, then plain rice, khichdi, boiled potato, plain toast, banana, chicken broth, and plain yogurt (probiotic). The key principles are: easily digestible, low fat and fibre initially, regular small meals, and advancing to normal diet as quickly as tolerated. Prolonged strict BRAT diet is not recommended as it lacks protein and nutrients needed for gut mucosal healing.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What foods cause food poisoning most often?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The highest-risk foods are: (1) Poultry (especially chicken) — Campylobacter and Salmonella; (2) Raw shellfish (oysters, clams) — Norovirus, HAV, Vibrio; (3) Raw or undercooked eggs — Salmonella; (4) Ground beef burgers — STEC E. coli O157:H7; (5) Ready-to-eat deli meats and soft cheeses — Listeria; (6) Reheated rice — Bacillus cereus; (7) Home-preserved/canned foods — Botulism; (8) Raw milk and unpasteurised dairy — Campylobacter, Salmonella, Listeria; (9) Raw sprouts — Salmonella, E. coli; (10) Pre-packaged salads — Norovirus, E. coli, Listeria.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is there a specific test to tell exactly what caused my food poisoning?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, though testing is not required for mild self-limiting illness. Stool culture identifies specific bacteria (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella) but takes 48-72 hours and has ~50-70% sensitivity. Stool multiplex PCR panel tests for 20+ pathogens simultaneously in 2-6 hours with >90% sensitivity (BioFire FilmArray is the most comprehensive). Stool antigen tests rapidly detect Giardia, Cryptosporidium, norovirus, and rotavirus. Blood cultures for bacteraemia (typhoid, Listeria). Widal test for typhoid. Stool for ova and parasites (3 samples) for Giardia, Entamoeba. The incubation period and food history together often predict the likely organism even before testing.

myths_and_facts.myth: You can tell if food is contaminated by its smell or appearance.
myths_and_facts.fact: Many dangerous bacteria (like Salmonella and E. coli) do not change the taste, smell, or look of food. When in doubt, throw it out.

myths_and_facts.myth: Reheating food always makes it safe.
myths_and_facts.fact: Reheating kills bacteria but does NOT destroy heat-stable toxins from Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus. Improperly stored food can still cause illness after reheating.
Drinking alcohol does not kill foodborne bacteria. The concentration consumed is far too low to have any antibacterial effect in the digestive system.

myths_and_facts.myth: Lemon juice or vinegar makes raw food safe.
myths_and_facts.fact: Acidic ingredients slow bacterial growth but do not reliably kill all pathogens. Raw fish marinated in citrus (ceviche) still carries risk.
Freezing stops bacteria from multiplying but does not kill them. Bacteria become active again when food thaws.

myths_and_facts.myth: Food poisoning always comes from the last meal you ate.
myths_and_facts.fact: Some pathogens like Listeria and Hepatitis A have incubation periods of weeks. The meal that caused illness may have been consumed days or weeks earlier.

faq.question: What is food poisoning?
faq.answer: Food poisoning (also called foodborne illness) is a sickness caused by eating food or drinking water contaminated with harmful bacteria, viruses, parasites, or toxins. It typically causes stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea.

faq.question: What are the symptoms of food poisoning?
faq.answer: Common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea (sometimes bloody), abdominal cramps, fever, headache, and fatigue. Symptoms range from mild to severe and may last from a few hours to several days.

faq.question: How soon do symptoms start after eating contaminated food?
faq.answer: Onset varies by pathogen: Staphylococcus toxins cause symptoms within 30 minutes to 6 hours; Salmonella takes 6–48 hours; E. coli 3–4 days; Listeria 1–4 weeks. Most common cases begin within 2–6 hours.

faq.question: How long does food poisoning last?
faq.answer: Most mild to moderate cases resolve within 1–3 days. Serious infections like Listeria or E. coli O157:H7 can last a week or longer and may require medical treatment.

faq.question: What causes food poisoning?
faq.answer: Food poisoning is most commonly caused by bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria, Campylobacter), viruses (norovirus, hepatitis A), parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium), and toxins from bacteria or naturally occurring in certain foods.

faq.question: How is food poisoning treated at home?
faq.answer: The most important step is replacing lost fluids. Drink water, oral rehydration solutions, clear broths, or diluted juice. Rest and avoid solid food until vomiting settles, then try bland foods like toast, rice, and bananas. Avoid dairy, caffeine, and fatty foods during recovery.

faq.question: When should I see a doctor?
faq.answer: See a doctor if you have a high fever, bloody stools, diarrhea lasting more than 3 days, signs of severe dehydration, nervous system symptoms, or if the affected person is an infant, elderly, pregnant, or immunocompromised.

faq.question: How can I prevent food poisoning?
faq.answer: Follow the 4 core principles: Clean (wash hands and surfaces), Separate (keep raw and cooked foods apart), Cook (to safe internal temperatures), and Chill (refrigerate promptly). Avoid unpasteurized products and raw/undercooked meat, eggs, and seafood.

faq.question: Is food poisoning contagious?
faq.answer: Some viral causes like norovirus and hepatitis A can spread person-to-person through poor hand hygiene. Most bacterial causes are not directly contagious but can spread through contaminated surfaces or shared food.

faq.question: What are the most dangerous complications of food poisoning?
faq.answer: The most dangerous complications include severe dehydration, hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS, which can cause kidney failure — especially in young children), botulism (paralysis), Guillain-Barré syndrome, and pregnancy complications such as miscarriage from Listeria.
